The Battle of Kuli-Malik was a major engagement in the long-standing military and political conflict between the Shaybanids (Uzbeks) and the Timurid ruler Babur. It took place in April 1512 in Transoxiana near Lake Kuli-Malik (possibly the modern-day Tudakul), close to Bukhara.
Background
At the beginning of 1511, taking advantage of the chaos following the death of Shaybani Khan, Babur launched a military campaign, capturing Hissar before advancing westward. By the summer of that year, he captured Bukhara, one of the most important Shaybanid cities. During this campaign, large numbers of people joined Babur's army, viewing him as the legitimate ruler of Transoxiana. In October 1511, Babur conquered Samarkand. However, in the Samarkand mosque, a khutbah was read in the name of the Safavid ruler Shah Ismail I, which greatly outraged the Sunni population of the city.
The Shaybanids initially hesitated to launch a counter-offensive. At a decisive moment, representatives of the Sunni clergy convinced them to defend the foundations of the Sunni faith. Meanwhile, Ubaydullah Khan, the ruler of Samarkand Muhammad Timur Sultan, the ruler of Tashkent Suyunchkhoja Khan, and the ruler of Fergana Janibek Sultan fled north to the city of Turkistan, where they were received by the local ruler Kuchkunji Khan.
The most active proponent of a counter-strike was the exiled ruler of Bukhara, Ubaydullah Khan. In April 1512, he gathered the people at the square of the Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi in Turkistan, calling them to war and publicly vowing to "undoubtedly reclaim sacred Transoxiana." Among the Shaybanids, he was supported only by the rulers of Samarkand and Fergana; the others did not believe in success.
The three rulers organized a joint military campaign southward and crossed the Syr Darya river. In late April 1512, an allied force of 3,000 men under Ubaydullah Khan's command reached Gijduvan, besieged it, and then moved to Bukhara to begin its siege. The governor of Bukhara sent messengers to Babur in Samarkand. Babur gathered an army of 40,000 and headed west to relieve Bukhara, supported by the Safavid State.
Learning of the enemy's movement, Ubaydullah Khan resorted to a ruse. He unexpectedly retreated to the northwest, feigning a panicked flight. The defenders of Bukhara believed the Shaybanids were retreating toward Khwarazm. The governor sent word to Babur that "the Uzbeks have retreated," which eased Babur's concerns, though he continued his march toward Bukhara.
The Battle
Ubaydullah Khan did not retreat to Khwarazm but instead hid his forces in the Kyzylkum Desert near Bukhara. His army was joined by several thousand locals dissatisfied with Babur's rule. Meanwhile, Babur reached the shores of Lake Kuli-Malik via Malikrabot. Suddenly, Ubaydullah Khan's army emerged from the steppe and struck Babur's forces. In the ensuing fierce battle, Babur's army suffered a crushing defeat. With his remaining forces, Babur retreated east back to Samarkand.
Aftermath
A day after returning to Samarkand, Babur learned that Ubaydullah Khan had captured Bukhara and was preparing to attack Samarkand. Babur, along with his family and close associates, fled to Hissar. Ubaydullah Khan captured Samarkand and had the khutbah read in his own name to mark the victory.
The historian Fazlallah Khunji Isfahani notes in his work Suluk al-Mulk that Ubaydullah Khan, as a gesture of decorum, granted the title of Supreme Khan and the throne of Samarkand to his uncle Kuchkunji Khan (a grandson of Mirza Ulugh Beg), while dividing the remaining lands of Transoxiana among other relatives.
Babur, having lost all his lands in Transoxiana, retreated south across the Amu Darya and was forced to seek further assistance from the Safavid ruler Shah Ismail I.
